credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
caption: Meteosat-9 SEVIRI, 21 December 2010. The tilted day–night boundary gives the Southern Hemisphere longer days. Axial tilt, rather than a change in Earth–Sun distance, controls this seasonal illumination.

credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
alt: Meteosat view of Earth's nearly north–south day–night boundary at the March equinox.
caption: Meteosat-9 SEVIRI, 20 March 2011. The terminator passes close to both poles around the equinox; refraction and the Sun's finite disc mean observed daylight is not exactly twelve hours everywhere.

credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · ECOSTRESS, PIA25423 · underlying map attribution retained in image · resized
alt: ECOSTRESS thermal map shows warm urban surfaces in London late at night on 15 July 2022.
caption: ECOSTRESS measured London's land-surface temperatures near midnight on 15 July 2022. Built surfaces remained warmer than many vegetated areas. These are surface temperatures, not standard air-temperature readings.

credit: USGS · public domain · 14 August 2021 ShakeMap · resized
alt: USGS ShakeMap of the 14 August 2021 Haiti earthquake with coloured zones of shaking intensity.
caption: USGS ShakeMap for the 14 August 2021 Haiti earthquake. Intensity varies from place to place and describes shaking effects; magnitude describes the earthquake's overall size. This is the published event-time map, not live hazard information.

credit: NOAA NCEI / CIRES · EMAG2 v3 · public domain · resized
alt: EMAG2 global magnetic-anomaly map with alternating anomalies across the ocean floor.
caption: NOAA EMAG2 v3 combines satellite, ship and airborne magnetic measurements. Oceanic magnetic stripes record spreading and changing polarity. Colours represent anomalies in nanoTesla, not directly the ages of rocks.
